0faec68c7b.q: How should leaders navigate AI adoption without losing focus on core business problems?
0faec68c7b.a: Leaders should go back to first principles: what problem are we trying to solve and how does the tool serve that problem. Too often, leaders and organizations mandate AI tool adoption without clarity on purpose. Instead, select tools aligned to your vision and strategy while recognizing that whatever tool you choose today will be different 90 days from now. Leaders should not try to keep up with every new AI development; instead focus on solving specific problems and creating real customer value.

0b8e6a683b.q: How is AI hiding weak performers and making performance evaluation more difficult?
0b8e6a683b.a: AI is raising the tide so your weakest performer gets better, but it's suddenly making 80% the good enough standard. The barrier to entry is much lower, and people are just bobbing along. People are being prepped for AI interviews and saying things that aren't true, and it takes time to snuff them out. For great leaders with human discernment to ask the right questions and assess real talent beyond what the machine tells someone to do, this is an advantage. But for leaders going along to get along, the noise and overwhelm means people can fake it easier than ever before.

6811d4b508.q: What is the risk of convergence to mediocrity as organizations adopt AI broadly?
6811d4b508.a: AI makes it easier to play at a surface level and harder to go deeper because we are used to getting good results fast. When we converge to the middle, everybody gets good at 80% quickly but loses the capability and strength to get great by going deep. The truly exceptional leaders will be those who go deep, hone their craft, and use AI diligently as a tool rather than as a replacement for thinking. Those who build processes intentionally, battle-test them, and then use AI to move faster will differentiate, while those using AI to replace original thinking will eventually fall off.
